etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English passionat, from Medieval Latin passionatus, perfect past participle of passiono (“to be affected with passion”). Equivalent to passion +‎ -ate (adjective-forming suffix). Compare French passionné.

definitions.definition: Given to strong feeling, sometimes romantic, sexual, or both.

quote.citation: 1718, Matthew Prior, Solomon, and other Poems on several Occasions, Preface, in Samuel Johnson (editor), The Works of the English Poets, London: J. Nichols, Volume 31, 1779, p. 93,[1]
quote.text: Homer intended to shew us, in his Iliad, that dissentions amongst great men obstruct the execution of the noblest enterprizes  […]  His Achilles therefore is haughty and passionate, impatient of any restraint by laws, and arrogant of arms.

quote.citation: c. 1596 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life and Death of King Iohn”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i], line 544:
quote.text: She is sad and passionate at your highness’ tent.

quote.citation: c. 1590–1591 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Two Gentlemen of Verona”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii], line 124:

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From a substantivation of the above adjective. Equivalent to passion +‎ -ate (noun-forming suffix).

quote.citation: 1804 (published; written in 1751), Samuel Richardson, The Correspondence of Samuel Richardson, volume III.182:
quote.text: When the passionates (forgive the word) break fences, leap from windows, climb walls, swim rivers.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From passion +‎ -ate (verb-forming suffix).

definitions.definition: (obsolete) To fill with passion, or with another given emotion.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book I, Canto XII”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC:
quote.text: Great pleasure mixt with pittifull regard, / That godly King and Queene did passionate [...].

quote.citation: c. 1588–1593 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Lamentable Tragedy of Titus Andronicus”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii], line 6:
quote.text: Thy niece and I, poor creatures, want our hands / And cannot passionate our tenfold grief / with folded arms.
